source_text: Cum haec itaque haud aliter quam dixi, constet impleta; mirari satis nequeo hominis impudentiam, qui in hoc recenti opere suo libros meos falsitatis accusat, quos tamen necdum in manus suas venisse testatur [n12] . Durum quidem, quod consuetudo peccandi amorem delicti facit; sed nihil durius, quam quod exstinguit pudorem; quod licet ex improbitatis usu esse constaret, tamen amplius praesentia pericula docuerunt, quam quisquam nostrum poterat autumare. Quando enim crederem eo usque Numidae induruisse frontem, ut in uno opere et uno versu utrumque fateretur, et me falsa dixisse, et se non legisse quid dixerim.
pass_a_gloss: Since therefore it stands that these things were fulfilled not otherwise than I said; I cannot wonder enough at the shamelessness of the man who in this recent work of his accuses my books of falsehood, which nevertheless he testifies have not yet come into his hands. Hard indeed, that the custom of sinning makes a love of the fault; but nothing harder than that it extinguishes shame; which, though it stood as being from the use of wickedness, yet present dangers have taught more than any of us could suppose. For when would I have believed that a Numidian's forehead had hardened to that point, that in one work and one line he would confess both, both that I had spoken false things, and that he had not read what I said.

lemmas.lexica: LS lex; Blaise lex Dei / sacred Law

pass_b_english: Since, then, it is established that these things were carried out just as I have said, I cannot sufficiently wonder at the man's shamelessness. In his recent work he accuses my books of falsehood, although he admits that they have not yet reached his hands (Augustine, On Marriage and Concupiscence 2.2). It is a dreadful thing that the habit of sinning produces a love of wrongdoing, but more dreadful still that it extinguishes shame. Although it was already clear that this comes from the practice of wickedness, our present dangers have taught us more about it than any of us could have supposed. When could I have believed that this Numidian's forehead had grown so brazen that in one work, indeed in one sentence, he would admit both that I had spoken falsely and that he had not read what I said?

choices.why: Julian means Scripture's legal/authoritative witness, especially the divine Law as teacher of justice.
rejected: natural law (unless the sentence is philosophical)

choices.why: Julian's ethical charge: habit of sinning kills pudor.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
